title: Mindfulness without ethics
hook: critics warn that mindfulness sold for productivity can lose its Buddhist ethical roots (Purser, 2019)

segments.voice: Yesterday: too many good results, and the drawer where flat studies go. Your line was a little sceptical. Did anything promise you a big change? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-seven.

A calendar invite lands in a work inbox. Mindfulness for peak performance. Twelve noon, conference room B, lunch provided. The pitch is simple: breathe, focus, reduce stress, get more done. Nothing wrong with any of that. But one critic asks a sharper question. What if the stress is coming from something that ought to change? A schedule nobody can meet. A boss who shouts. Then a practice that only teaches you to stay calm might be helping the problem stay put. Today is about that worry, and about where mindfulness came from before it reached the conference room.
screen: `MINDFULNESS FOR PEAK PERFORMANCE.` → `WHAT IF THE STRESS SHOULD CHANGE?` → `WHERE IT CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: First, the critique. Ronald Purser, a business professor and Buddhist teacher, wrote a book with a pointed title: McMindfulness. His argument is that mindfulness sold for productivity can be cut off from its roots, so it helps people adjust calmly to whatever is wearing them down, without asking whether that thing is right. Calm, he says, isn't the same as good. Second, the roots. In the Buddha's first teaching, as the tradition records it, right mindfulness is one part of an eightfold path. It sits beside right speech, right action and right livelihood: how you talk, how you act, how you earn a living. Mindfulness there is one strand braided with the others, not a tool that floats free of them. Third, a line that holds the strands together. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, sums up the teaching this way: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind." Purifying the mind comes last in that line, after not harming and doing good. Fourth, the other side, fairly. Defenders of secular programs say that leaving the religion out lets people in hospitals and offices try a practice they would never have tried otherwise, and that ethics can be taught without Buddhist doctrine. Buddhist teachers themselves differ: some welcome the secular programs, some share Purser's worry. Neither side is asking for less calm. The question is what the calm is for.
screen: `CALM ISN'T THE SAME AS GOOD.` · `ONE STRAND OF AN EIGHTFOLD PATH.` · `NOT HARMING, DOING GOOD, THEN MIND.` · `WHAT IS THE CALM FOR?` · then, large: `NOT JUST CALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give the calm a job. Before you settle, choose one ethical intention for today, in your own words, small and concrete. To speak without harshness in one hard conversation. To notice who is being left out of a meeting. To tell the truth about one small thing. Now settle, and let the breath slow. Rest with the breath for a while. Then, near the end, bring the intention back, once, and let the quiet you've gathered lean toward it. If you pray, you can offer it there. The bell holds the time.
Mindfulness without ethics. The critics' worry that a practice sold for productivity can lose the roots that tied it to how you treat people. Today's word.
Your line: not just calm. Today, when you notice you're calm, ask what the calm is for, and let it do the one thing you chose. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: In Buddhist teaching, mindfulness is practiced as one part of the eightfold path alongside right speech, action and livelihood; some secular teachers also pair mindfulness practice with an ethical intention for the day.

fork.setup: you've learned to stay calm and focused at work. in a meeting, a coworker is being treated unfairly. what does mindfulness, rooted in the eightfold path, ask?
options: stay calm and keep your focus on your own work.
notice clearly, and let it shape what you say and do.
step out of the meeting to breathe.
fork.reveal: in the eightfold path, mindfulness is braided with right speech and right action. the critics' worry is a calm that never reaches them.

original.note: Pali, from the Buddhist texts: mindfulness, also memory or keeping in mind. Right mindfulness is sammā-sati.

trapdoor: what you thought: mindfulness is a technique for staying calm and focused.
what it means: in the Buddha's teaching as recorded, mindfulness is one strand of a path that includes how you speak, act and earn.
what a scholar hears: Purser's McMindfulness critique turns on right mindfulness being one factor of eight, beside the ethical ones.

sources.ref: Ronald Purser, McMindfulness: How Mindfulness Became the New Capitalist Spirituality

sources.quoted: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind

notes: Confirm Purser's description: professor of management at San Francisco State University and an ordained Buddhist teacher (Korean Zen lineage). The voice says 'a business professor and Buddhist teacher'.
Confirm the Max Müller wording of Dhammapada 183: 'Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.' Only the first clause is quoted.
The eightfold path is named from the first discourse (SN 56.11) as 'the tradition records it'; only right speech, action, livelihood and mindfulness are named.
The defenders' view and the split among Buddhist teachers are given without ranking; no names or counts. Check the description is fair to secular program teachers.
Pali sati: confirm the note's glosses (mindfulness; memory, keeping in mind) and the Devanagari.
